hints: Start by picturing a photosystem in the thylakoid membrane - there is a central chlorophyll a reaction centre surrounded by many other pigment molecules. What job might those surrounding molecules do?

Think about wavelengths of light - if chlorophyll a alone can only absorb certain wavelengths well, how could a slightly different pigment help the plant harvest more light and what must happen to that extra energy?
walkthrough:
Not the Reaction Centre - The Helper**
Think of photosystem II and photosystem I sitting in the thylakoid membrane. Right in the middle is the reaction centre made of chlorophyll a - that is where light energy is actually converted to chemical energy when an electron is excited and passed to an electron carrier. Chlorophyll b sits around it in the light-harvesting complex. It never does that conversion itself, which is why we call it an accessory pigment.

Catching More Colours and Funnelling Energy**
Chlorophyll a absorbs red and blue light best but misses other wavelengths. Chlorophyll b has a slightly different structure so it absorbs different wavelengths that chlorophyll a misses. That extends the total range of light the plant can use. When chlorophyll b absorbs a photon, it passes that excitation energy on to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre. More light captured means a more efficient light-dependent stage.

Final answer: Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment. It absorbs wavelengths of light not absorbed by chlorophyll a, so extends the range absorbed, and passes the energy to the reaction centre / chlorophyll a, increasing efficiency of the light-dependent stage.

hints: Look first at the shape of each curve alone as light intensity rises from 0 to 1000 lux - where is it steep and where does it flatten?
Now compare the two curves vertically - which one is always on top, and does the gap stay similar at low and high light?
To earn full credit you need numbers - pick one light intensity in the rising part and one at the plateau, read off both rates with the full units $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Shared Pattern - Rise Then Plateau**
Both curves start at 0 and rise steeply at low light intensity. That tells you light is limiting the rate of photosynthesis. Then both flatten. For normal plants the plateau is around 155-160 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$ from about 700 lux onwards. For mutant plants the plateau is much higher, around 275 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$ from about 800 lux onwards. Flattening means something else other than light has become limiting.

Clear Difference - Mutant Always Higher**
At every light intensity above zero, the solid mutant curve lies above the dashed normal curve. The difference is present even at low light and gets larger at high light. This is a description, so you state what you see without explaining why yet.

Prove It With Numbers**
Always quote comparative data with units to support a graph description. For example, at 200 lux the mutant rate is about 130 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$ while the normal rate is only about 70 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$. At 400 lux the mutant is about 220 compared to about 120 for normal. At saturation, mutant plateaus near 275 and normal near 155 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$ - almost double.

Final answer: In both normal and mutant plants rate of oxygen production / photosynthesis increases with light intensity then levels off to a plateau. Mutant rate is higher than normal at all light intensities above 0. E.g. at 200 lux mutant approx 130 and normal approx 70 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$, at 800 lux mutant approx 275 and normal approx 155 $mmol mg^{-1} hour^{-1}$.

hints: Link back to (a) - if the mutant has extra chlorophyll b, what does that mean for total light absorbed at the same light intensity?
Follow the energy through the thylakoid - more light energy absorbed means more of which two short-lived products from the light-dependent stage?
Those two products drive the Calvin cycle in the stroma - what extra carbon compound will be made if the Calvin cycle can turn faster?
Think about what a plant must do to grow faster - where does extra glucose go to provide both energy and building materials?
walkthrough:
More Antenna Means More Light Captured**
The mutant contains more chlorophyll b, so at any given light intensity its light-harvesting complexes absorb more photons. That gives a faster rate of the light-dependent stage - more water split, more electrons excited in photosystems II and I.

More ATP and Reduced NADP to Drive the Stroma**
Faster photophosphorylation and faster reduction of NADP means more ATP and more reduced NADP are supplied to the stroma. These are the link between the thylakoid membranes and the Calvin cycle. More supply allows the Calvin cycle to turn over faster, fixing more carbon dioxide into more triose phosphate (TP).

More Sugar for Energy and Building**
Triose phosphate is converted to hexose sugars such as glucose. Some of that extra hexose is used in respiration, releasing more ATP to power cell division, active transport and other energy-requiring processes for growth. The rest provides carbon skeletons for biosynthesis.

Growth Is New Material**
Faster growth means making more cells and larger cells. That needs more cellulose for cell walls, more protein and amino acids for cytoplasm and enzymes, more lipids for membranes, plus starch for storage. With more photosynthate available, the mutant can synthesise more of all these, so it grows faster.

Final answer: More chlorophyll b absorbs more light, giving faster light-dependent stage. More ATP and reduced NADP made, allowing more turns of the Calvin cycle and more triose phosphate produced. More hexose made for respiration to release more energy for growth and for synthesis of amino acids, proteins, lipids, cellulose and starch.
